parts.note: surface reading: beginning a journey from Flint, a town in north Wales
setter's reading: a phrase meaning to set something going, as a flint striking steel sets a fire going

explanation.surface: A traveller sets out from the Welsh town of Flint.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes Flint look like a place name; read it as the stone that throws sparks when struck.
explanation.definitionFit: To spark off is to trigger or begin something, exactly what a struck flint does to tinder.

clue.text: Cabinet ministers arc — naturally not to brighten their prospects

definitions.text: Cabinet ministers arc — naturally not to brighten their prospects

parts.words: Cabinet ministers arc — naturally not to brighten their prospects
parts.note: surface reading: government ministers whose careers are unlikely to look any rosier
setter's reading: members of the opposition's shadow cabinet, whose prospects are darkened by their very title

explanation.surface: Government ministers face gloomy career prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arc' is a misprint for 'are'. The opposition's spokesmen form the shadow cabinet, so their prospects are, naturally, shadowed rather than brightened.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadowed means darkened or overcast, the opposite of brightened, and also suits the shadow cabinet.

clue.text: What don't they know? God knows

definitions.text: What don't they know? God knows

parts.words: What don't they know? God knows
parts.note: surface reading: an exasperated shrug about some ignorant people
setter's reading: the one thing these people hold cannot be known is God himself

explanation.surface: Someone throws up their hands at how little a group of people knows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God knows' is usually an idiom for 'nobody knows'; here it is the literal answer to the question.
explanation.definitionFit: These thinkers hold that the existence of a deity is unknown and perhaps unknowable.

clue.text: Snarls like Kay when the family's around?

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: kin is family; the possessive 's supplies the S
Kay is the spoken name of the letter K

explanation.surface: A woman named Kay turns snappish whenever her relatives visit.
explanation.walkthrough: Kay looks like a person, but it is just the letter K, sitting inside KIN'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Snarls are tangles or twists in a line or thread, which is what kinks are as a plural noun.

clue.text: A fair leg can easily be broken

definitions.text: A fair leg can easily be broken

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into pieces that can be put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shapely leg is easily snapped.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the description of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something delicate, easily snapped or damaged, is described as frail or brittle, which is what fragile means.

clue.text: Austere country for pictures in the spring

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, enclosed

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring
pictures are works of art

explanation.surface: A traveller goes to a strict, plain country for its spring paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: A spa is a resort built around a mineral spring, so 'spring' here is water, not the season.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek city-state was famed for its harsh discipline, giving us the word Spartan.

parts.note: surface reading: a bird offered as food for an elephant
setter's reading: a word that names an extinct North American pigeon and also someone carried on a jumbo jet

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to feed a pigeon to an elephant called Jumbo.
explanation.walkthrough: The passenger pigeon was a North American bird hunted to extinction; Jumbo is the jumbo jet, not the elephant.
explanation.definitionFit: A traveller carried aboard an aircraft, and the first word of a once-numerous American dove species.

indicators.note: to disrupt is to throw into disorder, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Troops take measures to destabilise Burma.
explanation.definitionFit: A dance is a sequence of steps, and this one is a Cuban ballroom dance.

indicators.note: beheading cuts off the head, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a magnate is a powerful tycoon

explanation.surface: A relative decapitates a tycoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The spear side is an old term for the male line of a family, as opposed to the distaff side.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnate is a kinsman descended through the male line of ancestry, from a common forefather.

clue.text: Has an interest in being warmly clad

definitions.note: the clue is a verb phrase; the answer is the participle, as in 'vested in'
definitions.meaning: first meaning: holding a legal right or stake
second meaning: wearing an undershirt to keep warm

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys being dressed snugly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has an interest in' looks like the clue's verb; it is one meaning, and 'warmly clad' is the other. A vest in British English is a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A vested right is legally secured to its holder, and someone wearing a woollen undershirt is literally dressed in one.

clue.text: Where's that Miss Laurie with the tankard? …

definitions.note: asks for a place, so it stands for a place name

parts.note: Annie Laurie is the heroine of the Scottish song; Ann is her first name
with means together with
a tankard holds ale

explanation.surface: A drinker asks after the girl from the old Scottish ballad while holding a beer mug.
explanation.walkthrough: Annie Laurie came from Dumfriesshire in south-west Scotland. The trailing dots run on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Annandale is a valley and district of Dumfriesshire in Scotland, and also a Sydney suburb, so it answers a 'where'.

clue.text: … Is returning with her man the cellarer

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written
Annie Laurie is Scottish, and mon is the Scots form of man

explanation.surface: Continuing the ballad: the girl comes home with her sweetheart, the wine steward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Simon the Cellarer' is a popular Victorian song about a wine-cellar keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title character is named as keeper of the cellar, so the cellarer of the song is this man.

clue.text: Such love as is no mirage we hope

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A romantic hopes that their love is real and not an illusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Desert travellers see illusory water; a fertile watering place in the desert is the real thing they hope to reach.

clue.text: Ominous predicament of the old noblesse

definitions.text: Ominous predicament of the old noblesse

parts.words: Ominous predicament of the old noblesse
parts.note: surface reading: the plight of a fading aristocracy
setter's reading: French nobles carried to the guillotine in tumbrils during the Revolution, which gave the idiom for being in trouble

explanation.surface: The old aristocracy finds itself in a threatening situation.
explanation.walkthrough: A tumbril is a farm cart; condemned French aristocrats rode in them to the guillotine. The British idiom means being in serious trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in deep trouble, literally the position of condemned nobles riding to execution.

parts.note: surface reading: something appears unfavourable
setter's reading: a thing that literally looks, with malicious intent

explanation.walkthrough: 'looks bad' normally means appears unpromising; here the thing does the looking, and with ill will.
explanation.definitionFit: A malevolent glance believed to cast a curse or bring misfortune on whoever receives it.

parts.note: surface reading: the call to rouse a sleeper
setter's reading: anything that startles someone into sudden awareness

explanation.walkthrough: Literally waking someone, the phrase stands for a revelation that makes them see clearly.
explanation.definitionFit: A surprising revelation that jolts someone into seeing a truth they had missed.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large sandbank in the North Sea
second meaning: one who dogs, or tails, a suspect

explanation.walkthrough: Dogger Bank is a shallow fishing ground in the North Sea, familiar from British shipping forecasts.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandbank named in shipping forecasts, and a tracker who follows a quarry closely like a hound.

clue.text: Look at that anti-protea protectionist, Herb

parts.note: to eye something is to look at it
John Bright, the Victorian free-trade campaigner against protectionist corn laws; 'protea' looks like a misprint

explanation.surface: Someone points out a man opposed to trade protection, named Herb.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bright led the Anti-Corn Law League against tariffs protecting British farmers. Herb looks like a man's name but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyebright is a small wild flowering plant, Euphrasia, once used as a remedy for sore eyes.

parts.note: surface reading: someone asks a cardinal why
setter's reading: by what means one reached a height, eminence being a summit

explanation.surface: Someone casually asks a cardinal for a reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How come' usually means 'why'; read literally it asks how you arrived. 'Your Eminence' is how cardinals are addressed, but an eminence is also high ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reaching a summit or high rank has climbed or risen there.

parts.note: surface reading: a full case of arrows
setter's reading: trees whose leaves are full of trembling

explanation.walkthrough: A quiver is an archer's arrow case, but here 'quiverful' means full of quivering, as these trees' leaves shake in the slightest breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Poplar trees whose flattened leaf stalks make their foliage tremble constantly, hence quaking or trembling poplars.

parts.note: a bird that perched has sat
a samovar is a Russian tea urn

explanation.surface: A planet balanced on top of a Russian tea urn.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece perched on another sits above it.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixth world from the Sun, the ringed gas giant of our solar system.

parts.note: surface reading: aggressive street sellers
setter's reading: things that scrape shins, since to bark a shin is to graze it, and also showmen who call out to passers-by

explanation.surface: Pushy sellers resort to violence on their customers' legs.
explanation.walkthrough: To bark your shin is to scrape the skin off it, so a shin-kicker is a barker of shins; a barker is also a fairground tout.
explanation.definitionFit: Showmen who stand outside fairground attractions shouting to draw in customers are touts of a kind.

parts.note: to become is to come to be
a team is a side

explanation.surface: Groups likewise turn into teams.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean additionally or moreover, adding one further point to what has already been said.

parts.note: surface reading: an invitation to attempt making something
setter's reading: to try is to make an attempt, and the noun is what one makes

explanation.walkthrough: 'one' seems to refer to some object; it is the very thing you make when you try.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt or exertion; to try hard is to make one of these.

parts.note: surface reading: nobody showed anyone the way to a girl
setter's reading: Wordsworth's Lucy dwelt among untrodden ways, so no walkers' tracks reached her

explanation.surface: No one guided anybody to Lucy.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem begins 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways', Lucy living where no trodden tracks went.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracks worn or laid for walkers; untrodden ways are those without such tracks.

parts.note: surface reading: a cold, unfeeling young woman named Green
setter's reading: a fruit with a stone at its heart, also a girl's name and a shade of green

explanation.surface: A heartless woman called Miss Green.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the fruit has a stone, Miss signals a girl's name, and Green is the colour it names.
explanation.definitionFit: The small fruit has a hard stone inside, gives its name to a dull green, and is a woman's name.

parts.note: surface reading: inept diplomacy
setter's reading: a state vessel, a heavy ceremonial boat, which is a clumsy craft to steer

explanation.walkthrough: Statecraft normally means the art of government; split it as state craft, a ceremonial river boat, and a lumbering one.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat-bottomed, slow, heavy vessel, including the ornate state ones used for royal processions on rivers.

parts.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a gap in it
setter's reading: William Collins's Ode to Evening fills the gap with an old word for embroidery or braid

explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation from William Collins's Ode to Evening; the missing word is an archaic form meaning embroidery.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic or poetic word for braid or embroidery, here the woven trimming of evening's cloudy skirts.

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
an ion is a charged particle

explanation.surface: A golden speck floats in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The hunter constellation, one of the most conspicuous star groupings visible overhead at night.

definitions.note: a noun; the answer is the adjective naming this kind of partridge
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the French partridge species with red legs
second meaning: French infantry wore red trousers at the start of the First World War

explanation.surface: A game bird resembles a veteran French soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Poilu was the nickname for a French infantryman, who went to war in 1914 in conspicuous scarlet trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: The common European partridge with crimson legs, and the scarlet-trousered French infantryman of 1914.

clue.text: They get nothing right in this — no practice?

indicators.note: to get things in is to take them inside, so the outer word encloses them

parts.note: taken as written
nothing is zero, shaped like O
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: People acquire nothing correct here, with no hands-on experience.
explanation.walkthrough: THE(OR)Y: the two letters sit inside the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstract principles as opposed to hands-on application, the familiar contrast between ideas and doing.

clue.text: Agreed to change to sand tees

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer consents to switch to tees made of sand.
explanation.walkthrough: Before wooden pegs, golfers teed the ball up on a little pile of sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean said yes or consented to a proposal.
